title: Room and House
premise: Sable Vane's late-night call-in show has been receiving calls from the recently dead for fifteen years, a secret they've buried under rational explanations. When a home sleep-recording app captures a second voice in Sable's apartment — a voice that answers questions no one asked aloud — they trace it to the Hollow House, a rooming house where, in 1974, six tenants were harvested for their identities by the landlord, Elias Thorn, who wears the stolen selves to stay alive. Sable discovers they were born in that house and that their own name is a borrowed one, stitched from a child who died there. The voice belongs to Wren, the child Sable once was, who wants their name back. On the night of the harvest moon, Sable returns to the house, gives up the stolen name and the false memories built on it, and lets the six harvested tenants — their found family across death — finally go, surviving as no one in particular, which is the first honest thing they've ever been.
about_author: Noor Lockridge is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years answering calls from strangers at 3 a.m. and never quite believed all of them were living. They write horror about houses that keep receipts, and live in a rented room they have never fully trusted.

chapters.title: The Dead Line
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. On the overnight show, a caller describes her own drowning from last Tuesday, and Sable does what they always do: thanks her warmly and moves on. We establish the ritual of denial — the show, the apartment, the fifteen years of explanations. Emotional beat: practiced numbness cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: Static Between Teeth
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A caller who identifies himself as Sable's father — dead since 2009 — asks why Sable never says their real name on air. Sable hangs up, shaken, and can't remember what name he means. Emotional beat: a hairline fracture in a carefully built identity.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, interleaved with the sleep recordings. The recording app captures Sable talking in their sleep — and someone answering, a small voice asking, 'Do you still have it?' Sable plays it forty times and hears their own mouth reply, 'Yes.' Emotional beat: dread arriving not as a scream but as a question.

chapters.title: Room 3B
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Digging through a storage unit of their late mother's things, Sable finds a lease dated 1974 for a rooming house — the Hollow House — signed by a woman named Maren Vane, with a child listed as a tenant: Sable Vane, age four. Sable has no memory before age six. Emotional beat: vertigo of a past that doesn't add up.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In the old neighborhood, an elderly man recognizes Sable's face and calls them by another name — 'Little Wren' — then flees when asked about 1974. Sable learns six tenants vanished that year and the landlord, Elias Thorn, was never charged. Emotional beat: the first solid evidence, and it's worse than mystery.

chapters.title: The Voice Has a Name
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first time — a child's voice in the walls of the Hollow House, watching Thorn wear the faces of the harvested, waiting. She knows the radio voice is hers. Emotional beat: patient, terrible hope.

chapters.title: Calls from the House
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The show's dead callers begin all asking the same thing: 'Come back to the house.' One recites Sable's childhood address. Sable's producer hears the calls too — the first witness. Emotional beat: relief of being believed, terror of what's believed.

chapters.title: Thorn's Voice, Borrowed
chapters.summary: Thorn's POV. Elias Thorn, 101 years old and wearing his sixth stolen identity, feels the harvest moon approaching and the seams of his stolen selves fraying. He hears Wren's voice in the walls and knows the debt is being called. Emotional beat: a predator discovering he is prey to something older than his crime.

chapters.title: The Producer's Tape
chapters.summary: Sable and producer Dev's shared POV. Dev plays Sable a recording of last night's broadcast: during the dead air, Sable's voice answered questions in a child's cadence. Dev, whose own brother's voice called the show last month, chooses to stay and help. Emotional beat: found family forming in the dark.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Explaining
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A quiet chapter of excavation: Sable maps every 'coincidence' of their adult life — jobs, loves, moves — and sees how the false name shaped everything. They confront the possibility that they are not the person they've mourned being. Emotional beat: grief for a self that may never have existed.

chapters.title: The House Lets You In
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, first visit. The Hollow House stands renovated and occupied, its tenants pleasant and interchangeable, all with the same laugh. The current landlord — young, wrong, Thorn's face under a younger one — invites Sable in for tea and asks, gently, if they've brought it back. Emotional beat: politeness as horror.

chapters.title: Wren in the Walls
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reaches through to Sable in the house, showing her the night of 1974 in fragments: Thorn's ritual, the six tenants folded into him, and herself — hidden, unfinished, left behind because she was already half-gone. Emotional beat: the child's loneliness underneath the haunting.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In the house's basement, Sable finds the harvest room and six name-plates, one reading WREN VANE. They understand: to free the dead, the stolen name must be returned — which means unmaking the self they've lived as. Dev begs them not to go through with it. Emotional beat: the price named out loud.

chapters.title: The Interchangeable Tenants
chapters.summary: Multiple tenants' POV, braided. The house's current residents — people who moved in and slowly stopped being distinct — describe the comfort of dissolving, and warn Sable that Thorn doesn't need the moon to harvest, only consent. Emotional beat: seduction of surrender, power's soft corruption.

chapters.title: Thorn Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Sable and Thorn's alternating POV. Thorn offers Sable the deal he offered everyone: keep the name, keep the life, and help him harvest Wren properly before the moon. He shows Sable the warm, easy eternity of the house. Sable, exhausted by fifteen years of holding, is tempted. Emotional beat: the villain's most human moment.

chapters.title: Dev at the Door
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev, followed by the house's tenants, arrives to drag Sable out and instead finds Sable mid-ritual, half-dissolved into Wren's memories. Dev speaks Sable's chosen name — the one they made for themselves on air, the one listeners loved — and it holds. Emotional beat: a name given freely as an anchor.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The moon rises. The house unfolds — rooms rearranging, the six harvested surfacing in Thorn's skin, screaming to be let out. Thorn, unraveling, tries to take Wren by force. Sable must choose in minutes what they've dodged for fifteen years. Emotional beat: terror compressed to a single decision.

chapters.title: The Returning
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable speaks their own unmaking: gives back the name Wren Vane, surrenders the false memories, and holds the child as the six tenants pour out of Thorn, who collapses into a heap of borrowed faces and finally, mercifully, no one. Emotional beat: loss and liberation in the same breath.

chapters.title: Six Goodbyes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, dawn. The freed dead, including Wren — now a whole ghost, then no ghost at all — thank Sable and go. Wren's last words: 'You were never me. You were the one who carried me.' The house goes quiet and ordinary. Emotional beat: mourning that finally ends.

chapters.title: No One in Particular
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Legal and existential aftermath: no records of who Sable 'really' is, and for the first time it doesn't frighten them. They rebuild a small, chosen life — a name on the show's marquee that belongs to no dead child. Emotional beat: identity as something made, not found.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, on air. The final broadcast: the phone lines are silent of the dead, and Sable tells the listeners, live, a version of the truth. A caller — alive, ordinary, lonely — asks how you start over with no past. Sable answers: 'You let someone hand you a name.' Emotional beat: the show becomes what it always pretended to be.

chapters.title: Room and House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, coda — the child in the house before 1974, before everything, happy for one ordinary evening, unaware. The reader now knows what's coming and holds her in it. Final line: the house keeping its one warm memory, the only thing it never harvested. Emotional beat: tenderness as the last word of a horror story.
